transcript.text: Hi there! I'm PersonaAI, and we'll figure out your type through a quick chat. To start, tell me about a time recently when you had to tackle a big project or a deadline. What did your approach look like?

I just grabbed some scrap wood and got straight to work fixing my back deck when the rot set in last weekend. Didn't make a plan on paper, just figured out what needed replacing as I went. Talking about it just wastes daylight.
I love that hands-on, jump-right-in approach! When you hit a tricky spot on the deck where nothing fit quite right, how did you decide what to do next?
I just measured the gap twice, grabbed the saw, and trimmed the board down until it fit right into place. No point overthinking it when you can see the problem right in front of you.

Measuring twice and trusting what's right in front of you makes total sense. Now, tell me about a time you had to give someone feedback or news they really wouldn't like. What went through your mind and what did you actually do?

I just told my neighbor straight up that his fence was encroaching on my driveway by six inches. No need to sugarcoat it or make a big dramatic thing out of it. We just moved it back over a beer that same afternoon.
Direct and practical, keeping things moving smoothly! After a particularly long, demanding week filled with projects and interactions, what does your ideal evening look like to unwind, and why?

I usually head out to the garage to tinker on my old motorcycle with some classic rock playing quietly. It's quiet out there, and turning a few wrenches helps clear my head without having to deal with anyone's drama.
When you're out there working on the motorcycle or taking on a new project, what kinds of things spark your curiosity about how they work or how you could improve them?

I usually wonder if I can swap out a stock part for something heavier-duty that I can machine myself in the corner. If something feels flimsy or overly complicated, I just want to tear it down and rebuild it simpler and tougher.
